items.text: Difference between legal wrong and moral/social wrong

segments.text: A crime is conduct that the law treats as an offence against the state or public order and for which a legal punishment may follow.

This area asks you to understand what makes conduct criminal. A good answer separates the legal definition from morality. In criminal law, the usual starting point is a prohibited act or omission plus the legally required mental element, subject to the wording of the offence and available defences.

Criminal law does more than describe behaviour that society dislikes. It identifies conduct that the state has chosen to prohibit through law and attaches public consequences such as conviction, punishment, supervision or another criminal sanction. This is why the principle of legality matters: a person should not be punished for conduct unless the law defined the offence before the conduct occurred.

A useful way to understand criminal liability is to separate the physical and mental dimensions of an offence. The physical dimension is often called the actus reus. It may consist of a positive act, an omission where the law recognizes a duty to act, a prohibited circumstance, a prohibited result, or a combination of these. The mental dimension is often called mens rea. Depending on the offence, the required state of mind may involve intention, knowledge, recklessness, negligence, dishonesty or another legally defined mental element. These expressions are not interchangeable; the wording of the particular offence controls.

A disciplined criminal-law analysis normally moves through a sequence. First, identify the offence and its statutory ingredients. Second, ask whether the accused performed the prohibited conduct. Third, connect any prohibited result to that conduct through the required rules of causation. Fourth, identify the mental element required by the offence and determine whether it existed at the relevant time. Finally, consider general exceptions, special defences and any rule that reduces the grade of liability.

The same physical event can therefore lead to different legal consequences depending on intention, knowledge, circumstances and available defences. A death caused deliberately, a death caused with knowledge of a dangerous consequence, and a death caused by negligent conduct may all involve a human death but are not legally identical.

Crime and tort can arise from the same event, but they ask different legal questions. Criminal proceedings focus on public responsibility and penal consequences; tort proceedings ordinarily focus on a civil wrong and a remedy such as damages. A breach of contract arises from failure to perform a legally enforceable voluntary obligation. A moral or religious wrong may be socially or ethically important but does not automatically become a crime unless positive law criminalizes it.

This distinction is important because legal systems should not be described as if every undesirable act belongs to the criminal law. Criminalization is a particularly serious form of state regulation because it may authorize arrest, trial, stigma and punishment.

Hypothetical illustration: suppose a driver strikes a pedestrian. The fact of injury does not by itself answer the criminal-law question. The investigator and court would need to examine the driver’s conduct, the applicable traffic or penal provision, the required mental state, causation and any legally relevant circumstances. The example shows why criminal liability is ingredient-based rather than outcome-based.

items.text: an act becomes a crime because a valid law prohibits it and attaches a criminal consequence. Moral dislike by itself does not create a criminal offence.

Separate the external part of an offence from the mental part. The external part may be an act, an omission where law imposes a duty, a result, and a causal link. The mental part may involve intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence depending on the offence.
Always ask whether a defence or general exception applies. A person may perform the physical act but still escape liability if the law recognizes a valid justification or excuse.

For comparison questions, explain the nature of the wrong and the usual remedy: crime concerns public wrong and punishment; tort usually concerns civil injury and compensation; breach of contract concerns failure of a voluntarily assumed legal obligation.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not write that every immoral act is a crime or that every crime requires the same mental element. The exact ingredients depend on the offence.

items.text: Learn a short legal definition of crime.
Understand act/omission, intention or knowledge, causation and punishment at a basic level.
